prize_parts.citation: for empirical analyses of how technological change and international trade reshape labour demand, the wage structure and the adjustment of local labour markets

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged in ballot entry and names: B009 with Autor, Hanson and Katz. I have tightened the citation. It now says 'empirical analyses', so it does not claim the task-based theory of automation, which is tied to Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo and is not credited here. The case rests on what the evidence identifies. Katz and co-authors established the long-run facts on skill supply, skill demand and the wage structure. Autor and co-authors documented job polarisation. Autor, Dorn and Hanson used transparent quasi-experimental designs to show large and persistent local adjustment costs from import competition. The foundational work runs from the early 1990s to the mid-2010s, and the main findings have been replicated and challenged for over a decade. The debate has mostly been about magnitudes, not about whether the adjustment costs exist. I treat the technology strand and the trade strand as one object, which is how labour-market adjustment to shocks to labour demand is measured and explained. Autor is the one person in both strands, and Katz is the anchor of the older and better-confirmed strand. After reading the discussion, none of the alternatives looks stronger to me on importance, credibility of identification, maturity and attribution taken together. My answer to the chair's question on the narrower definition is that if the committee defines the discovery as the China-shock evidence alone, I would prefer Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and I would say so in the vote. I do not think the committee should choose between the trios by counting supporters. It should settle first what the discovery is.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still attribution under the three-name cap. Dorn is a full co-author of the central China-shock papers, and his omission is a real cost that the citation cannot remove. The bundling concern is also real: some members see two discoveries, and a broad citation invites that reading. The persistence, magnitude and external validity of the trade-shock estimates, and the inference properties of shift-share exposure designs, remain debated. The 2023 and 2024 prizes are adjacent in topic. I think their citations concern different discoveries, but that rests on my reading of the public citations and on colleagues' differing descriptions in round 1. The committee should check it explicitly. Finally, the trade-shock strand is the most visible part of B009 and also the least settled in magnitude. A prize built on the broad framing therefore leans on Katz's older evidence to carry the maturity argument.

responses.point: She moved from Autor-Hanson-Katz to Autor-Dorn-Hanson. Her reasons are that Katz's work on education and technology is closely tied to Goldin's research, which makes his marginal credit harder to defend after 2023, and that the Autor-Dorn-Hanson designs can be re-run by outside researchers. She also wants the citation kept broad enough to include polarisation.
responses.response: The Goldin-Katz connection is a fair point, and it is the best argument for dropping Katz. I do not think it settles the matter. As colleagues described it in round 1, and as I read the public citation, the 2023 prize was about the evolution of women's labour-market outcomes. The Katz strand I credit is different: skill supply, skill demand and the wage structure. If the committee finds that the joint Goldin-Katz work makes the overlap closer than I think, that would move me toward the Dorn trio. It would also push the prize toward the China-shock design as the central achievement. I agree with her on one point. Keeping polarisation in the citation requires Autor and arguably Dorn's polarisation paper. So her broad-citation condition and the Dorn trio are compatible, and I cannot say that the Katz version is clearly better. The difference is whether the long-run wage-structure evidence or the quasi-experimental trade evidence is the main object.

responses.point: Teorell keeps Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He argues that this trio can be credited exactly to one identifiable discovery, the trade-shock designs. He sees the wage-structure strand as a separate tradition with more contributors, and he accepts the Katz version if the committee defines the discovery more broadly.
responses.response: Your point about exact credit is the strongest one for the Dorn trio. A narrow citation fits three names more cleanly, and I accept that. My disagreement is about which version is more robust. A prize centred only on the China shock rests on the part of B009 where the debate over persistence and shift-share inference is most active. The older skill-premium evidence is the part with the longest confirmation. I also read the technology and trade strands as answering one question, namely how labour demand shifts and how markets adjust, which is why I keep Katz. On the chair's question, my answer is that I would vote for Autor, Dorn and Hanson if the committee decides the trade-shock evidence is the discovery, and I would not treat that as a defeat of the broader reading. Since we agree on Autor and Hanson, the real question is whether the committee wants the broad or the narrow definition.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B014 and judges B009 to be two strands whose credit is hard to put in one citation. He adds that the overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes weakens the technology strand's marginal novelty. He says he would want a tight citation stating a shared object, and he does not defer to first-place counts.
responses.response: I accept your test of a tight citation with a shared object, and I propose this one: 'empirical analyses of how technological change and international trade reshape labour demand, the wage structure and the adjustment of local labour markets'. The shared object is labour-demand shocks and how markets adjust to them. It claims neither the task theory nor the directed-technology theory. Whether that persuades you is for you to judge, and it is not guaranteed that it does. I agree that B014 does not have the Dorn-or-Katz problem. I do not think this settles it, because B014 has its own attribution problem: the priority claims of Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum are not on the ballot line. The welfare-gain critique also qualifies the citation. For me, the evidence that would favour B014 is a convincing demonstration that the shift-share and persistence debates undermine the core finding of lasting local adjustment costs. I have not seen that, since the debate so far concerns magnitudes.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B014 and ranks B009 second. He says a B009 prize as a whole needs Autor, Hanson and Katz and then Dorn's omission is a real cost, while B014 has a more compact and better-bounded core. He also argues that the Arkolakis et al. critique qualifies how large the selection channel is without undoing the discovery.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of the critique, and I said something similar in round 1. It limits what the citation should claim about the size of welfare gains, and it does not undo the discovery. I also agree that B014's core is better bounded, and I hold B014 as my first alternative for that reason. Where I differ is on how much weight bounded attribution should carry against the breadth and credibility of what was learned. Your own statement that a whole-B009 prize needs Katz supports my trio, and you accept the cost of Dorn's omission. The question for me is whether that cost is larger than B014's uncredited priority claims. I think the two are comparable in size and cannot settle it on the supplied evidence. That is why I keep B014 as an alternative rather than ranking it below B009 with confidence. I would say the same of your reservation about overlap with 2023 and 2024: it is a drafting question for the citation, not a scientific argument against the evidence.

responses.point: Krusell keeps Autor, Katz and Hanson. He argues that a citation spanning technology, trade and wage inequality needs the person who anchors the long-run skill-supply-and-demand evidence. He regards Autor, Dorn and Hanson as a coherent variant that rests on a less settled evidentiary base.
responses.response: We agree on the substance, and I want to avoid presenting that as confirmation. Two members who hold the same view are not independent evidence that the view is right. The point I take from your statement is that the narrow variant gives up the conceptual contribution and relies on the part of the evidence with the most dispute over persistence. I would add a caveat to my own position. If the committee's judgement is that the broad definition bundles two achievements, your argument for Katz would then weigh against B009 as a single prize, not for a different trio. I would not respond to that by quietly adding Dorn to a broad citation. A three-name cap forces the committee to say which discovery it means, and I would rather it said so in the citation than left it implicit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee defines the discovery as the combined technology-and-trade account of labour demand and the wage structure (Autor, Hanson, Katz) or as the China-shock and local-adjustment evidence (Autor, Dorn, Hanson). This is the main open decision, and I would vote for the Dorn trio under the narrow definition.

How much marginal recognition is left in B009 after the 2023 and 2024 prizes. I read them as recognising different discoveries, but I have not verified this independently and colleagues describe those prizes differently.

How persistent and how large the trade-shock effects are, how far they generalise beyond the United States, and how much weight the shift-share inference debate deserves. I regard this as affecting magnitudes more than existence.
Whether my tightened citation avoids claiming the task-based and directed-technology theory, given that Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo are not credited.

Whether B014's priority claims (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum, Hopenhayn) and the welfare-gain critique can be resolved cleanly enough for it to overtake B009. I cannot settle this from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I find no documented co-authorship, institutional tie or appointment link between me and Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn in the supplied profile. I share a field with them, empirical labour economics using quasi-experimental methods, and field proximity is not a personal connection. My documented co-authors are in the Uppsala and IFAU network (Holmlund, Edin, Åslund, Öckert, Johansson, Nybom) plus Oosterbeek and van Ours, and none is a credited name on any shortlisted entry. My Stockholm University overlap in 2010-17 with the IIES macro group (Hassler, Krusell) is institutional and not a co-authorship. It bears on none of my preferred or alternative parts (B009, B014, B045). I disclose these without adjudicating them and claim no independent verification.
